posts.title: Catch failures in production AI agents
posts.promise: Turn agent traces into grouped findings and a human-reviewed root-cause report.
posts.whatItIs: Tessary is an open-source tool for teams running AI agents in production. Its repository describes receiving traces (records of an agent’s operations), checking them with classifiers, grouping related findings into cases, and investigating likely causes using trace evidence and, when connected, repository code. A small student project could accept test traces, apply a few simple checks, group matching alerts, and prepare a report for a developer. Teams operating AI agents are a plausible customer, but the sources do not establish who pays. The repeating work is trace checking and case preparation; a person still needs to confirm whether a finding is a real problem and choose any fix.
posts.whoPays: Hypothesis: teams operating production AI agents may pay for help finding and investigating failures; the repository does not establish paying customers or revenue.
loop: Receive an agent trace through an instrumentation endpoint.
Normalize the trace into a consistent format.
Run enabled classifiers and open findings when checks trigger.
Group related findings into a case.
Investigate the case using trace evidence and connected repository code when available.
Send the findings and explanation to a human owner, who decides whether and how to fix the system.
posts.evidence: The official repository describes an open-source agent reliability platform that monitors traces, uses classifiers to detect issues, groups related findings into cases, and runs root-cause investigation over trace and optional repository evidence. It also says the product hands alerts to a human and does not open the fix. These statements describe the project; they do not independently establish accuracy, adoption, or revenue.
posts.uncertainty: The available evidence is the project’s repository description, not independent reliability testing. A student MVP could use sample traces and a few transparent checks; it would not reproduce production scale or prove that alerts identify real failures. Trace data can contain sensitive information, so a demo should use synthetic or consented data. A human must validate findings and approve any change.
first24Hours: Create synthetic traces for one test agent, including a successful run and a deliberately failing run.
Write two simple checks and group matching findings into a case record.
Generate a report that links each alert to the trace evidence and asks a person to review it.
